title: Guaranteed Structured Outputs & Schemas
summary: Write one JSON Schema that survives three constrained decoders: what OpenAI, Claude, and Gemini structured outputs actually guarantee, the schema subset all three accept, SDK helpers that rewrite your schema, and the refusal, truncation, and casing failures a guarantee does not cover.
objectives: State precisely what constrained decoding guarantees on each provider -- schema-shaped output -- and what it leaves to the application.
Design a schema inside the subset that OpenAI strict mode, Claude structured outputs, and Gemini structured output all accept, and enforce the constraints they drop with local validation.
Use Zod or Pydantic SDK helpers without letting the schema the model sees drift away from the schema your code enforces.
Detect and handle refusals, truncation, enum-casing drift, and inputs that cannot produce a valid answer.

sections.title: What 'guaranteed' actually guarantees
paragraphs: All three providers can now constrain generation to a JSON Schema you supply. OpenAI Structured Outputs makes the response adhere to the schema, so the model cannot omit a required key or invent an enum value; in the Responses API it is enabled with a `text.format` of type `json_schema` and `strict: true`. OpenAI recommends it over the older JSON mode, which guarantees valid JSON but not schema adherence. Claude structured outputs use constrained decoding: `output_config.format` with type `json_schema` returns JSON matching your schema in the response's text block, and `strict: true` on a tool definition applies the same guarantee to tool inputs. Gemini produces responses that adhere to a supplied JSON Schema when you request `application/json` output with a schema.

The guarantee is about shape. OpenAI notes that Structured Outputs can still contain mistakes, and that the model will always try to fit the schema -- which can produce hallucinated values when the input has nothing to do with it. Google's best-practice list says the same thing more briefly: the output is syntactically correct JSON, so always validate the values in your application.

Two operational details follow from how Claude builds the guarantee. It compiles each schema into a grammar: the first request with a new schema pays compilation latency, compiled grammars stay cached for 24 hours from last use, and changing the schema's structure invalidates that cache while changing only names or descriptions does not. Anthropic also injects a system prompt describing the expected format, which costs input tokens. And because schemas are cached separately from message content, Anthropic states that PHI must not appear in schema property names, `enum` or `const` values, or `pattern` expressions.
sections.callout: Schema-valid is a statement about syntax and types. Correct, grounded, and authorized are still your job.

sections.title: The schema subset all three will accept
paragraphs: Each provider accepts a different subset of JSON Schema, and the differences are not cosmetic. OpenAI strict mode requires every property to appear in `required` (emulate an optional field with a type union such as `["string", "null"]`), requires `additionalProperties: false` on every object, forbids a root-level `anyOf`, and supports `$defs` and recursive schemas as well as `pattern`, `format`, `minimum`/`maximum`, and `minItems`/`maxItems`. It does not support `allOf`, `not`, or `if`/`then`/`else`, and it caps a schema at 5,000 object properties and 10 levels of nesting.

Claude structured outputs allow optional properties but count them: at most 24 optional parameters and 16 union-typed parameters across all strict schemas in one request, and at most 20 strict tools. `additionalProperties` must be `false`; recursive schemas, numeric constraints such as `minimum` and `maximum`, string length constraints, and array constraints beyond a `minItems` of 0 or 1 are not supported and return a 400. Property order follows the schema except that required properties come first. Gemini documents `enum`, `format`, `minimum`/`maximum`, `minItems`/`maxItems`, `prefixItems`, and nullable type arrays, lets `additionalProperties` be a boolean or a schema, and warns that very large or deeply nested schemas may be rejected.

The portable core is therefore narrow and predictable: an object at the root; every property required, with `null` in a type union where a value may be absent; `additionalProperties: false` on every object; string enums; `$defs` only where reuse needs it, and no recursion; and no numeric or length constraints in the schema you send. Keep those constraints -- they are real business rules -- but enforce them in a local validation step after the response arrives. Making every property required also settles ordering: OpenAI emits keys in schema order and Claude emits required keys first, so an all-required schema comes back in one order from both.

sections.title: SDK helpers rewrite your schema -- validate against the original
paragraphs: Hand-maintained JSON Schema drifts away from the types your code actually uses. OpenAI strongly recommends the SDKs' native Pydantic (Python) and Zod (JavaScript) support, or a CI step that regenerates the schema from the types or the other way round. The helpers look alike across providers: OpenAI's JavaScript SDK pairs `responses.parse` with `zodTextFormat` and returns `output_parsed`; Anthropic's TypeScript SDK pairs `messages.parse` with `zodOutputFormat` (or `jsonSchemaOutputFormat` without Zod) and returns `parsed_output`; Google's structured output guide shows the same pattern with Pydantic in Python and Zod in JavaScript, parsing the returned text locally.

Read what a helper does before trusting it. Anthropic documents that its Python, TypeScript, Ruby, and PHP SDKs transform a schema that uses unsupported features: they remove constraints such as `minimum` and `maxLength`, append each removed constraint to the field description, add `additionalProperties: false` to every object, filter string formats to the supported list, and then validate the response against your original schema. The model sees the relaxed schema; your code still enforces the strict one. OpenAI takes the opposite approach with `strict: true` and rejects an unsupported schema with an error -- which is why a Zod discriminated union, which produces a root-level `anyOf`, fails there.

Your own validator needs the same scrutiny. In JSON Schema 2020-12, `format` is an annotation by default: the specification requires implementations that can assert formats to keep that behavior disabled unless it is switched on, so a local validator may accept `"not-an-email"` for `format: "email"` without complaint. Omitting `additionalProperties` allows any extra property, and `required` asserts only that the named keys are present. Decide explicitly which of these your local check enforces, then prove it with a deliberately bad payload.

code.label: One source of truth, enforced after the response

sections.title: Refusals, truncation, and casing: what still reaches your code
paragraphs: Constrained decoding cannot stop the model from refusing or from running out of tokens, and either one produces output that does not match your schema. Claude signals a safety refusal with `stop_reason: "refusal"` and HTTP 200, bills the tokens it generated, and lets the refusal message take precedence over the schema; a cut-off response has `stop_reason: "max_tokens"` and may be incomplete, and Anthropic's remedy is to retry with a higher `max_tokens`. OpenAI returns a `refusal` content item in place of schema output, and marks truncation with `status: "incomplete"` and an `incomplete_details.reason` of `max_output_tokens`. Check these signals before you parse, not after the parser throws.

Some drift is quieter. Anthropic documents that structured outputs do not guarantee the capitalization of string `enum` and `const` values: the model may return a value that differs from the schema only in case -- typically the first letter of a word after a space -- with no error and no special stop reason. Compare enum values case-insensitively and never define two values that differ only by case. Anthropic also lists structured outputs as incompatible with citations (a 400) and with message prefilling.

Finally, give the model a legitimate way out. Because the model always tries to satisfy the schema, OpenAI advises telling it in the prompt what to return when the input cannot produce a valid response. Build that answer into the schema itself -- an `"other"` category, a null field, a `needs_human` flag -- so that 'this email is not a support ticket' does not come back as a confidently filled-in ticket.
sections.callout: Look at stop_reason, status, and refusal items first. JSON.parse is the last step, not the error handler.

activity.title: Port one extraction schema across three providers
instructions: Take one real extraction task and write its schema once, inside the portable subset: object root, every field required with null unions for absent values, additionalProperties false, string enums, and no numeric or length constraints.

Move every dropped constraint (lengths, ranges, formats) into a local validator generated from the same source of truth, and prove that it rejects a payload with a malformed email, an over-length summary, and an extra property.
Send the schema through OpenAI strict mode, Claude output_config.format, and Gemini structured output. Record every 400 error and the schema change that fixed it.
Force each failure path in a test: a request that should be refused, a max-token limit too low to finish, an input unrelated to the schema, and an enum value returned in the wrong case.
evidence: The single-source schema, the relaxed schema actually sent to each provider, and the local validator, with the three rejected test payloads.
A failure-path table listing provider, induced failure, the exact signal observed (stop_reason, status, refusal item, or casing), and how the code handled it.
activity.reflectionPrompt: Which constraint in your schema was the model never shown, and what would have reached your database if your local validator had not enforced it?

questions.prompt: What does OpenAI Structured Outputs with strict: true guarantee that JSON mode does not?
choices: Valid JSON syntax
Adherence to the supplied schema, such as required keys and enum values
Factually correct values
Lower latency
questions.explanation: Both produce valid JSON; only Structured Outputs ensures schema adherence. Neither guarantees that the values are correct.

questions.prompt: A schema uses maxLength on a string and minimum on an integer. What happens when Anthropic's TypeScript SDK sends it through zodOutputFormat?
choices: The API enforces both constraints during decoding
The SDK removes the unsupported constraints from the sent schema, notes them in the descriptions, and validates the response against the original schema
The constraints are ignored everywhere
The SDK falls back to JSON mode
questions.explanation: Anthropic documents this transformation for its Python, TypeScript, Ruby, and PHP SDKs: the model sees a relaxed schema while the SDK still enforces the original constraints.

questions.prompt: Which schema pattern is portable to OpenAI strict mode, Claude structured outputs, and Gemini structured output?
choices: Optional properties left out of required
A root-level anyOf discriminated union
Every property required, with null in a type union for values that may be absent, and additionalProperties false
A recursive schema that references the root
questions.explanation: OpenAI requires every property to be required and forbids a root anyOf, and Claude does not support recursion. The required-plus-nullable pattern is accepted by all three.

questions.prompt: Claude returns stop_reason "refusal" with HTTP 200 on a structured-output request. What is true?
choices: The text block is still guaranteed to match the schema
The output may not match the schema, the generated tokens are billed, and the application must handle the refusal before parsing
The request was not billed
Retrying with a higher max_tokens fixes it
questions.explanation: The refusal message takes precedence over schema constraints. A higher max_tokens addresses max_tokens truncation, not a refusal.

questions.prompt: Your local JSON Schema validator accepts "not-an-email" for a field declared with format: "email". Why can that be correct behavior?
choices: format is always an assertion in JSON Schema
In JSON Schema 2020-12, format is an annotation by default and assertion has to be enabled explicitly
email is not a defined format
Validators never check strings
questions.explanation: The validation specification requires format-assertion behavior to be disabled by default, so enable it or check the format in code.

questions.prompt: Claude returns "Access" for a string enum declared as ["billing", "access", "bug", "other"]. What does Anthropic advise?
choices: Treat it as a schema violation and retry until the case matches
Compare enum values case-insensitively, and avoid enum values that differ only by case
Switch the field to free text
Add a pattern to force lower case
questions.explanation: Structured outputs do not guarantee the capitalization of enum and const values, and the response completes normally with no error or special stop reason.
